title: Explain a race-condition fix
Report benchmark numbers
text:
I reran our search API benchmarks after switching the ranking step from per-document scoring to batched scoring. Same hardware (c7g.2xlarge), a 10k-query replay, 3 runs each, medians below. Write up the results for the PR description.

Before (per-document): p50 41 ms, p95 118 ms, p99 260 ms, throughput 1,850 req/s, CPU 78%, memory 1.9 GB.
After (batched, batch size 32): p50 29 ms, p95 71 ms, p99 192 ms, throughput 2,640 req/s, CPU 64%, memory 2.3 GB.

I also tried batch size 64: p50 31 ms, p95 69 ms, p99 240 ms, throughput 2,700 req/s, CPU 66%, memory 2.8 GB.

title: Compare three storage options
text:
We need somewhere to keep user-uploaded attachments for the support app: about 2 TB today, growing about 150 GB a month, mostly PDFs and screenshots under 5 MB, read a few times in the first week and rarely after that. Compare these three options and tell me which you'd pick.

1. Postgres large objects in our existing database: no new service; backups get much bigger (the nightly dump already takes 40 minutes); database storage costs $0.115/GB-month.
2. S3 Standard with a lifecycle rule to S3 Infrequent Access after 30 days: $0.023/GB-month, then $0.0125/GB-month; $0.0004 per 1,000 GETs; needs signed URLs and a new IAM role; 99.99% availability.
3. A self-hosted MinIO cluster on our three existing storage nodes: no per-GB bill, but about 6 hours a month of ops time; we'd handle disk failures and upgrades ourselves; nobody on the team has run it before.

title: Needs the person's decision between two rollout plans
text:
We're rolling out the new billing engine next week and I have two plans on the table. Tell me which you'd recommend and why; I'll make the call.

Plan A, percentage rollout: 5% of accounts on Monday, 25% on Wednesday, 100% the following Monday. Both engines run during the rollout, and a flag can send any account back to the old engine in under a minute. It costs about 3 extra days of dual-running infrastructure (around $1,200). Risk: if we roll an account back mid-cycle, that customer gets invoices from two engines in the same month.

Plan B, cut over by billing cycle: every account whose cycle starts on the 1st moves on 1 December; the rest move at their next cycle start over the following 4 weeks. No account ever has two engines in one cycle. Rolling back means waiting for the next cycle or re-running invoices by hand (about 2 hours of finance time per 100 accounts). It takes 4 weeks to finish instead of 1.

Finance prefers B; support prefers A.

title: Explain a schema migration
text:
Can you explain what this migration changes and what someone running it in production needs to watch for? The users table has 4.2M rows and orders has 31M.

Old schema:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT NOT NULL,
  name TEXT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id),
  total NUMERIC(10,2),
  status TEXT
);
```

New schema:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  display_name TEXT,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  total_cents BIGINT NOT NULL,
  status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'paid', 'refunded', 'cancelled'))
);
CREATE INDEX orders_user_id_idx ON orders(user_id);
```

title: Explain a request flow across services
text:
I'm new on the team. Can you explain how a password-reset request flows through our services? Here's what I've pieced together from the code:

- The web app POSTs /password-reset to the API gateway with the email.
- The gateway rate-limits by IP (5 per hour) and forwards the request to the auth service.
- The auth service looks the user up in Postgres. If there is no such user it still returns 202, so nobody can probe for registered emails.
- If the user exists, auth creates a reset token (32 random bytes, stored hashed, expires in 30 minutes) and publishes a password_reset_requested event to the message queue.
- The notification service consumes the event, renders the email template and sends it through the email provider. On a provider error it retries 3 times with backoff, then moves the event to a dead-letter queue.
- When the user clicks the link, the web app POSTs /password-reset/confirm with the token and the new password. Auth checks the hash and the expiry, updates the password, deletes the token and revokes all of that user's sessions.
